synopsis: For brake-commanding functions on earth-moving machines, the corpus identifies ISO 19014, using MPLr, rather than ISO 26262 as the functional-safety framework; awareness-only systems are excluded from ISO 19014-2, but issuing brake commands crosses that scope boundary [f2071, f2196, f11985, f11986]. Adding automatic braking therefore changes the safety-engineering scope: targets should come from hazard analysis rather than matching the warning system, and validation must address faults, degraded modes, missed braking and unintended braking beyond perception performance [f5221, f11989, f5223, f5810, f11089]. Required evidence spans control hardware, software and environmental qualification, including documented safety-function performance under expected environmental conditions [f1098, f7735]. Planning should confirm standards applicability early with a qualified functional-safety specialist and map the minimum evidence package to the October 2026 editions; all five ISO 19014 parts were due for reissue that month, shortly before design verification freezes, while several cited sources remain marked draft or under revision [f9787, f11099, f12000, f6548, f1098]. Cybersecurity, configuration control and software updates become safety-relevant when software commands brakes, but ISO 19014-4 excludes cybersecurity, and no incident statistics quantify these risks, so separate safety and cybersecurity processes are needed rather than unsupported accident frequencies [f3664, f10820, f3665, f3666]. The corpus also flags a planning gap: the eight machine-motion and brake-timing questions omitted functional safety and integrity level, while the skeptic's review objects to treating the new safety-control function as an incremental feature [f6579, f10515].

Changed safety-engineering scope supports the objection to treating braking as an incremental feature.
